title: Clusters, sharing, and twins
subtitle: A Joint Bob node can belong to any number of clusters. Membership alone shares nothing: a node shares chosen projects or whole workspaces with a cluster, and every member of that cluster receives them. Twins are the same user's machines and share everything they own. Changes travel through two hubs per cluster, and a twin can take over a machine that is gone for good.

items.heading: Membership
items.body: Every node creates an Ed25519 identity. A cluster's manager signs the member list; members are numbered by join order. A node can be a member of any number of clusters and presents one URL to all of them.

items.heading: What a peer may see
items.body: A peer sees a project if it is a twin of the project's owner, or it shares a cluster with the owner and the owner selected the project (or its workspace) for that cluster. Every member of that cluster receives it. Data outside any project, canvas shortcuts, push subscriptions, and ntfy servers go to twins only.

items.heading: Isolation between clusters
items.body: A node in clusters X and Y shares each project only with the cluster it selected. Members of X and Y do not learn about each other and cannot authenticate to each other.

items.heading: Twins
items.body: Twins are the same user's machines. Both sides consent: in Settings > Cluster, choose **Make twin** next to a node of a shared cluster, and that node's owner accepts the request; a node outside every cluster pairs by link instead. Afterwards each shares everything it owns with the other: projects, conversations, tasks, files, transcripts, credentials, routing configurations, and update rights.

items.heading: List filters
items.body: The **Clusters** filter above the project list shows projects shared through the chosen clusters, **Only on this node** for projects this node owns and shares nowhere, and **From twins** for projects a twin owns. Above the conversation list it filters by where the agent runs: **This node**, or another member of a chosen cluster. Choosing several options shows everything that matches any of them, and the same goes for the status chips and labels.

items.heading: Deleted conversations
items.body: Deleting a conversation removes its transcript on every node that holds a copy: when the deletion arrives, and at start-up for copies left behind by older releases. A deleted conversation is never offered or copied in again.

items.heading: Hubs
items.body: For each cluster, the node that makes a change sends it only to two hubs: the lowest and the highest numbered other members that answer. If a hub does not answer, the next member in line takes its place.

items.heading: Forwarding
items.body: A hub applies the change and forwards it to every other member of that cluster that may see it. Each relayed event carries its origin's signature; a hub cannot forge or alter it.

items.heading: Catch-up
items.body: Every node keeps each cluster event it holds in a relay log. At start-up and every minute a node pulls everything after its cursor from the two hubs, so a node that was offline, or missed a forward, catches up. A project shared with a cluster later sends its earlier events once, except usage and recent-conversation events past their retention window.

items.heading: Out-of-order events
items.body: Some events can only be placed once an earlier one has arrived, such as a conversation's ownership before its conversation record. A receiver sets such an event aside and applies it when it can, instead of refusing the batch. Events that never fit are dropped after 7 days.

items.heading: Twins
items.body: Twins keep direct delivery. A cluster whose other members are all twins of this node needs no hubs.

items.heading: Declare it lost
items.body: On a twin of the lost machine, open Settings > Cluster and, under This node and its twins, select **Machine lost** next to it. Only a twin can do this: the dual-signed twin certificate proves the lost machine trusted it.

items.heading: Ownership moves
items.body: The twin becomes the owner of everything the lost machine owned and reissues its sharing. Other members verify the certificate against the keys they already hold and accept the twin as the new owner.

items.heading: Clusters
items.body: The manager removes the lost machine. When the lost machine was the manager, the most senior remaining member takes over management and removes it.

items.heading: Rebuild
items.body: Install Joint Bob on the new or repaired machine and pair it as a twin with the survivor. It receives everything again. Invite it to its clusters again.

blocks.title: A lost manager without a twin
blocks.body: A cluster whose manager is lost and had no twin cannot choose a new manager. Keep the machine that manages a cluster twinned with another machine you own.

blocks.title: Git history on synced projects
blocks.body: Syncthing never copies `.git`, so a commit pushed from one node leaves the others' HEAD behind files they already have. Before every user message and goal turn, a node whose project is a git repository runs `git fetch` and moves HEAD and the index (never the files) to the upstream commit, but only when the files on disk already hold that commit, this node has no unpushed commits, and nothing is staged. Otherwise HEAD is left alone. A failed fetch is logged and the turn continues.

items: Every machine request is signed and checked against the sender's pinned key, a 60-second clock window, and a replay-proof nonce. Bearer machine tokens are no longer accepted anywhere.
Runtime calls are authorized by the project they name. A request for a project that is not shared with the caller returns 403.
Relayed events are accepted only with a valid origin signature, from a member of the cluster, for a project the receiver, the origin, and the sender may all see.
Only the lost machine's twin can succeed it. A succession notice from anyone else returns 403.
Remote update installation requires an active twin.
A connection that fails on malformed data closes that socket only; it never stops the node.
Update every node of a cluster to this release. Older nodes do not relay or pull, and reject member lists with more than five members.
Legacy bearer-token pairing is removed. A node that still has a legacy pairing loses it and must join through a cluster invitation or pair as a twin.
A node older than 1.59.0 must first upgrade to a release between 1.59.0 and 1.97.x.
The retired pairing tables are dropped on start; the node keeps its identity.

Every 15 minutes a node prunes its replication tables: usage events leave the outbox and relay log after 30 days, recent-conversation events after 7, inbox receipts after 14, and delivered hub queue rows after a day; a recent-conversation event repeated word for word by a newer one goes at once. Other event types are kept, so a node or project share added later gets only that much usage and recents history from other nodes.
An event a twin was refused and later becomes eligible for is sent at the next full outbox search, within about 5 minutes.
Shared agent skills (the agent-resources Syncthing folder) do not synchronize between nodes.
A node advertises one URL to all its clusters, so every cluster must reach it at that URL.
Tasks still assigned to a lost machine keep that assignment until they are handed off.

Git catch-up follows commits that reached the remote. A commit that was never pushed stays on its node, and its files appear as uncommitted edits on other nodes until it is pushed. Commits made in a terminal, outside a conversation, are picked up at that project's next user message.
